context: All three panels use nodes numbered 1 through 5. From left to right, arrows in the singly linked list and the tree represent directed references, and lines in the undirected graph represent adjacency in both directions. The panels compare three structures side by side rather than showing steps of an algorithm that transforms one into another.
description: Consider the connection rules from most to least restrictive. In a singly linked list, every node except the tail has exactly one successor, forming a single chain. In a tree, a parent can have multiple children, forming branches down from the root. Each nonroot node has exactly one parent, and connections cannot cross branches or form cycles. A graph dispenses with the root and hierarchy requirements. Any two vertices can be connected according to the relationship being modeled, and cycles are allowed.

The label “most freedom in how nodes connect” beneath the undirected graph on the right refers to its having the fewest connection constraints. It does not describe an algorithm's complexity. The table lists every connection in each structure.

frames.explanation: The undirected graph contains cycles such as 1—2—3—1 and 2—4—5—2. Vertex 3 has no edge to either 4 or 5, so the graph is not complete. Viewing nodes as vertices and references as edges lets us interpret linked lists and trees as graphs.
frames.title: Connections in linked lists, trees, and graphs

summary: The same five nodes illustrate a linear chain of successors, a branching hierarchy, and a network that allows connections across branches and cycles.
